title: Reynolds Number in Fluid Mechanics
short_intro: The Reynolds number is a dimensionless quantity used in fluid mechanics to predict flow patterns in different fluid flow situations. It represents the ratio of inertial forces to viscous forces within a fluid subjected to relative internal movement.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of Reynolds number, formula involving density, velocity, characteristic length, and viscosity, critical Reynolds number, and identification of laminar and turbulent flow regimes.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Dimensional analysis derivation of Reynolds number using Buckingham Pi theorem, transition limits in pipes and channels, and application to dynamic similarity models.

concept_notes.heading: Physical Significance of Reynolds Number
bullets: Represents the ratio of inertial force per unit volume to viscous force per unit volume in a flowing fluid.
Dimensionless quantity denoted by the symbol Re.
Determines whether a fluid flow will be laminar, transient, or turbulent.

concept_notes.heading: Flow Regimes in Circular Pipes
bullets: For Re < 2000, the flow is strictly laminar or streamline, characterized by smooth parallel layers.
For 2000 < Re < 4000, the flow is unstable and transitional between laminar and turbulent.
For Re > 4000, the flow is fully turbulent, characterized by chaotic eddies, cross-currents, and fluctuations.

concept_notes.heading: Inertial vs. Viscous Forces
bullets: Inertial forces originate from the momentum of the fluid elements and tend to maintain chaotic motion.
Viscous forces originate from intermolecular friction and tend to damp out disturbances and maintain ordered layer flow.
High viscosity or low velocity leads to domination of viscous forces, resulting in laminar flow.

concept_notes.heading: Dynamic Similitude and Scale Models
bullets: Two fluid systems are dynamically similar if their respective Reynolds numbers are equal.
Used extensively in aerodynamics and naval architecture to test scale models in wind tunnels or towing tanks.

derivations.title: Dimensional Analysis Derivation of Reynolds Number
derivations.conditions: Incompressible fluid flow through a straight circular pipe
steps: Identify the variables affecting the viscous force or frictional pressure drop: fluid density (ρ), dynamic viscosity (μ), flow velocity (v), and pipe diameter (d).
Express the functional dependence as a dimensionless product: π = ρ<sup>a</sup> v<sup>b</sup> d<sup>c</sup> μ<sup>d</sup>.

Substitute the fundamental dimensions [M], [L], and [T] for each variable: [M<sup>0</sup>L<sup>0</sup>T<sup>0</sup>] = [ML<sup>-3</sup>]<sup>a</sup> [LT<sup>-1</sup>]<sup>b</sup> [L]<sup>c</sup> [ML<sup>-1</sup>T<sup>-1</sup>]<sup>d</sup>.
Equate the exponents of fundamental dimensions M, L, and T to zero: For M: a + d = 0; For L: -3a + b + c - d = 0; For T: -b - d = 0.
Solve the system in terms of d to get a = -1, b = -1, c = -1, d = 1, leading to the combination μ / (ρ v d).

derivations.title: Force Ratio Derivation
derivations.conditions: Fluid element of characteristic length l, velocity v
steps: Inertial force F<sub>i</sub> ∼ mass × acceleration ∼ (ρ L<sup>3</sup>) × (v / t) ∼ ρ L<sup>2</sup> v<sup>2</sup>.
Viscous force F<sub>v</sub> ∼ shear stress × area ∼ (μ (v / L)) × L<sup>2</sup> ∼ μ v L.
Take the ratio of the inertial force to the viscous force: Re = F_i / F_v = \frac{\rho L^2 v^2}{\mu v L}.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Reynolds' Dye Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A schematic of a water tank with a glass pipe, introducing a fine filament of colored dye into the center of the water flow.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: At low velocities, the dye filament remains a straight distinct line (laminar). At higher velocities, the dye filament wavers and diffuses uniformly throughout the pipe (turbulent).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Demonstrates the physical transition from laminar to turbulent flow and defines critical velocity.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Moody Diagram (Friction Factor vs. Reynolds Number)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Log-log plot of Darcy friction factor (f) on y-axis against Reynolds number (Re) on x-axis for various relative roughness values.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows a linear decrease of f with Re in the laminar region, a sharp discontinuity in the critical zone, and independence of f from Re at very high Re in the fully rough turbulent zone.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Directly tested in PGT numericals relating pressure drop to Reynolds number in pipes.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Drag Coefficient vs. Reynolds Number for a Sphere
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Log-log plot of drag coefficient C<sub>d</sub> against Reynolds number Re for flow past a sphere.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Highlights Stokes' law regime (Re < 1), the Newton's resistance regime, and the drag crisis phenomenon around Re = 2 × 10<sup>5</sup>.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used to evaluate terminal velocity modifications in different fluid regimes.

solved_numericals.question: Water at 20°C (μ = 1.0 × 10<sup>-3</sup> Pa s, ρ = 1000 kg m<sup>-3</sup>) flows through a pipe of diameter 0.05 m with a velocity of 0.02 m s<sup>-1</sup>. Calculate the Reynolds number and state the type of flow.
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: ρ = 1000 kg m<sup>-3</sup>, v = 0.02 m s<sup>-1</sup>, d = 0.05 m, μ = 1.0 × 10<sup>-3</sup> Pa s.
Substitute values into the Reynolds number formula: Re = (ρ v d) / μ.
solved_numericals.answer: Re = 1000, which is less than 2000, hence the flow is laminar.

solved_numericals.question: An oil of density 900 kg m<sup>-3</sup> and kinematic viscosity 1.0 × 10<sup>-4</sup> m<sup>2</sup> s<sup>-1</sup> flows through a 10 cm diameter pipe. Find the maximum velocity for which the flow remains laminar (take Re<sub>critical</sub> = 2000).
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: ρ = 900 kg m<sup>-3</sup>, ν = 1.0 × 10<sup>-4</sup> m<sup>2</sup> s<sup>-1</sup>, d = 0.1 m, Re = 2000.
Use the kinematic viscosity form of the Reynolds number: Re = (v d) / ν.
Rearrange to solve for velocity: v = (Re × ν) / d.

solved_numericals.question: Air at standard temperature and pressure (ρ = 1.2 kg m<sup>-3</sup>, μ = 1.8 × 10<sup>-5</sup> Pa s) flows past a flat plate of length 2 m at a uniform speed of 5 m s<sup>-1</sup>. Calculate the Reynolds number at the trailing edge of the plate.
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: ρ = 1.2 kg m<sup>-3</sup>, v = 5 m s<sup>-1</sup>, characteristic length L = 2 m, μ = 1.8 × 10<sup>-5</sup> Pa s.
Apply the Reynolds number formula for a flat plate: Re = (ρ v L) / μ.

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumes Newtonian fluid behavior where dynamic viscosity remains constant regardless of the shear rate.
Critical Reynolds number limits (2000 and 4000) apply strictly to smooth, straight circular pipes and can vary significantly with pipe roughness and inlet disturbances.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Reynolds number has dimensions of velocity.
common_misconceptions.why: It is a ratio of two forces (inertial to viscous force), so all fundamental dimensions cancel out.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Transition from laminar to turbulent flow always occurs precisely at Re = 2000.
common_misconceptions.correct: Re = 2000 marks the upper limit of stable laminar flow, but turbulence typically initiates only after crossing a transition range up to Re = 4000.
common_misconceptions.why: Flow stability depends on upstream disturbances, surface roughness, and vibration levels.

quick_revision: Reynolds number (Re) is the ratio of inertial force to viscous force and is completely dimensionless.
Reynolds Number (Density form): Re = \frac{\rho v d}{\mu}
Reynolds Number (Kinematic Viscosity form): Re = \frac{v d}{\nu}
